newsitem.title: JAPAN: FEATURE - Japanese economy likely to tread water.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Japanese economy likely to tread water.

text.p: Japan's economy, which has been growing slowly since late 1993, is likely to tread water for a while after peaking in the first quarter of this year, economists say.
Economists do not see the economy starting to shrink in the near future, but neither do they expect it to pick up speed, at least in the next two years.

"The economic recovery since late 1993 has been supported only by big manufacturing firms. But the bulk of industries -- small manufacturers and non-manufacturing firms -- are still in the doldrums," said Johsen Takahashi, an economist at the Mitsubishi Research Institute.

Output by non-manufacturing firms accounts for nearly 65 percent of Japan's gross domestic product (GDP) -- total output of goods and services minus net income from overseas production -- which amounted to 500 trillion yen ($4.31 trillion) in 1996.
INTEREST RATES AT RECORD LOW LEVELS

Given the outlook, economists said the Bank of Japan (BOJ), the nation's central bank, was likely to keep interest rates at record low levels at least until later this year when economic data for the July-September quarter is due to be released.

Some say the BOJ may have to wait at least another year or so to correct what economists say are "abnormal" interest rate levels. The BOJ has kept the official discount rate, which it charges on loans to banks, at an historic low of 0.5 percent since September 1995 to support the economy.

"The only reason why the economy has been accelerating is because of ultra-low interest rates. I think they (BOJ) are trying to keep rates as long as possible to underpin the economy," said Andrew Shipley, an economist at Schroders Japan.
BOJ officials have said the bank will make sure the economic recovery is firmly in place before it considers changing the discount rate.

Optimists in financial markets expect the BOJ to raise the discount rate after confirming through the April-June quarter data that the economy has successfully withstood the negative impact from the April 1 increase in Japan's sales tax.
Many economists warned against this.
"I would advise against too much optimism regarding medium growth prospects," Shipley said.
Economists said fiscal tightening, sluggish private consumption, restraint in export drives and a possible slowdown in capital spending will prevent the economy from accelerating.
IMPACT OF FISCAL REFORM PLAN

Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto announced a plan on Tuesday to redress Japan's debt-ridden finances, including cuts in general expenditure and public works spending -- a measure to stimulate the economy traditionally taken by the government.

Takashi Kiuchi, chief economist at Long-Term Credit Bank of Japan Ltd, said the fiscal reform plan itself would push down GDP growth by 0.4 to 0.5 percentage points annually through to fiscal year 2003/04.

Mitsubishi's Takahashi said the rise in the sales tax, the ending of special income tax cuts in the current fiscal year, and an increase in social welfare fees would increase people's financial burdens by a total of nine trillion yen ($77.5 billion) in 1997/98.

"I don't think Japan's economy can sufficiently absorb the negative impact on private consumption of the nine trillion yen burden," Takahashi said. He predicts Japan's GDP will grow by 0.5 percent in 1997/98.

Economists polled by Reuters earlier this year forecast an average GDP growth rate of 1.7 percent in 1997/98 and 0.1 percent in 1998/99. The government is expected to achieve its official growth target of 2.5 percent for 1996/97.
PROFIT GAINS HELPED BY WEAK YEN
Capital spending, the other engine of the economy, along with private consumption, is expected to continue to grow on the back of better earnings in 1996/97.

However, some economists are sceptical whether capital spending will keep rising given the recent appreciation of the yen against the dollar, which would have a negative impact on earnings, especially those of major exporters.
Recent earnings reports by Japanese companies for the last business year show that their combined profits rose by more than 10 percent.

But Hiroki Matsushita, an analyst at Wako Research Institute of Economics, said it may be questionable to say that 1996/97 profit growth reflected a substantial improvement in corporate Japan's strength because much of the gains were heavily dependent on the weak yen.

The yen's sharp depreciation to over 127 yen to the dollar in early May from about 79 yen in April 1995 helped boost the earnings of Japanese exporters by making their products competitive in global markets.
However, the yen has rebounded against the dollar, to around 115 yen, which could have some negative effects on corporate earnings this year, eventually affecting their capital investment plans.
The only possible support to the economy could come from the continuation of strong exports and the implementation of economic reforms, economists said.

But Japan's brisk exports, helped over the past year by the weak yen and a strong economy in the United States, may not last forever as the yen has recently appreciated and U.S. growth is expected to slow down later this year, they said.
Besides, exporters may try to curb exports to the United States as Washington has warned Japan to prevent a significant rise in its external surplus.

Major carmaker Toyota Motor Corporation has announced that it plans to trim its car exports to the United States this year. A Toyota official denied media reports that the planned reduction was due to worries of renewed U.S.-Japan trade friction.
"One quarter or two quarters away, Japan's trade surplus will be fine (will not increase significantly) because U.S. growth will be slowing," Schroders' Shipley said.
The government hopes economic reforms will boost growth in Japan's GDP by an average of about 0.9 percent per year in the years from 1998/99 to 2003/04.
